# Skales

> Websites & systems for service businesses. Builds websites, online booking and follow-up automation for UK service businesses (trades and local operators). Run by Tom Griffiths, one person, in the United Kingdom.

Key facts:
- Builds websites, online booking and follow-up automation for UK service businesses (trades and local operators).
- One person: the person you message is the person who builds it.
- Thirty-six working demonstration builds run live on the site; every business in them is fictional.
- One system a week is built in public on Instagram.
- Clients own their domain, code and accounts from day one; nothing is rented back to them monthly.
- Every build is hand-coded with no page-builder, no theme and no third-party runtime dependencies.
- Contact: thomasrgriffiths08@gmail.com · Instagram @tomxsystems (https://www.instagram.com/tomxsystems/)
- Book a call: https://thomasrgriffiths08-blip.github.io/skales/book/

## Pages
- [Home](https://thomasrgriffiths08-blip.github.io/skales/): what Skales builds, with a live demonstration build on the page.
- [Work — thirty-six builds](https://thomasrgriffiths08-blip.github.io/skales/work/): every demonstration build, each running live and each with its own page.
- [Websites](https://thomasrgriffiths08-blip.github.io/skales/work/websites/): the four kinds of website (loud, motion, quiet, direct) with every example.
- [Tools](https://thomasrgriffiths08-blip.github.io/skales/work/tools/): the broad tools for any service business and the ones built for a single trade.
- [What I do](https://thomasrgriffiths08-blip.github.io/skales/what-i-do/): the three services — capture websites, online booking with a pipeline, missed-call and review automation — with the systems running, and the four-step process.
- [Why](https://thomasrgriffiths08-blip.github.io/skales/why/): ownership (clients own domain, code and accounts), one person, built in public, and the FAQ.
- [Book a call](https://thomasrgriffiths08-blip.github.io/skales/book/): four qualifying questions, then a slot straight into the diary.
- [Free teardown](https://thomasrgriffiths08-blip.github.io/skales/teardown.html): three details in, three findings back by message.
- [Notes](https://thomasrgriffiths08-blip.github.io/skales/notes/): short pieces — what a missed call actually costs a service business; why i don’t rent you your own website; sixteen builds for businesses that don’t exist, on purpose.

## The thirty-six builds
- [Northgate Quote Engine](https://thomasrgriffiths08-blip.github.io/skales/work/northgate-quote-engine/): business tool for an invented kitchen fitter — A quote that assembles itself while the customer answers.

- [SIGNAL 2027](https://thomasrgriffiths08-blip.github.io/skales/work/signal/): website for an invented music & light festival — Type that reacts to how hard you scroll.
- [Kerbside Scorecard](https://thomasrgriffiths08-blip.github.io/skales/work/kerbside-scorecard/): business tool for an invented google profile report card — Marks a Google Business Profile like an exam.
- [Stopcock](https://thomasrgriffiths08-blip.github.io/skales/work/stopcock/): business tool for an invented missed-call leak meter — What unanswered calls cost you a year.

## Frequently asked
- **Do I actually own the website?** Yes. With Skales the domain, the code and the hosting sit in your own accounts from day one. It is set up so you could walk away tomorrow and lose nothing; that is the whole point.
- **Is there a monthly fee to keep my site online?** No. Skales does not charge a monthly platform fee to keep your own website alive. You pay for hosting and your domain directly, in your own name, at cost. If any quote you get includes a monthly fee to keep your own site online, that is rent.
- **How long does a build take?** A capture website takes days. A full system with booking and follow-up usually takes one to two weeks. You get a date with the quote, and you can watch it being built in public.
- **Are the thirty-six builds on this site real clients?** No, and deliberately so. Every business, person, review and phone number in the demonstration builds is invented, so nothing on this site exposes anyone Skales works with. They are real working software, just for businesses that do not exist.
- **Who actually does the work?** Tom Griffiths. Skales is one person: there is no account manager and no handover to a junior. The person you message is the person who builds it.
- **What kind of businesses is this for?** UK service businesses whose work comes in by phone: plumbers, heating engineers, electricians, roofers, kitchen fitters, landscapers, cleaners, salons and similar trades and local operators.
- **What happens after I book a call or send the form?** Tom Griffiths looks at your website, your Google listing and what happens when someone tries to reach you, then messages you three things: what is leaking, what to fix first, and what it is worth in jobs. If you want it fixed, you get a flat quote. If not, you keep the list.
- **Do you use page-builders or templates?** No. Every build is hand-coded with no page-builder, no theme and no third-party runtime dependencies. Every visual is drawn in code rather than bought from a stock library.

All 12 Loud 3 Motion 3 Quiet 3 Direct 3 Loud Big, kinetic, confident. The type is the image and one moment does the talking. L O U D When does a business need a loud website? When being remembered matters more than being reassured. A boxing club or a tattoo studio is chosen on feel, so the site moves, the type hits and there is one thing the visitor will describe to a friend. Everything still works: the number, the booking and the address are one tap away. Motion The page is the film: scroll-driven sequences, letterboxes, timecodes, drawn frames. Reel 01 · 24 fps Motion 00:00:00:00 What does a website for a film or video business look like? Like a film. The visitor scrubs through the work by scrolling, the page carries a timecode, and nothing in it is a stock video: the frames are drawn in code, so the page weighs nothing and plays on a phone. The story reads even if you never scroll. Quiet Plain, calm, expensive. Almost nothing moves; the typography does the work. Quiet. Why would a business choose a plain website? Because its customers are buying trust, not excitement. A quiet page uses real typography, generous space and one accent, and moves exactly once. It is harder to make than a loud one, because nothing is hiding behind an animation. Direct Conversion first. One-tap call, a three-field form, the service area, no fluff. 0113 496 0000 Call now What does a tradesperson’s website actually need? The number, a form with three fields, proof you cover their street and a reason to ring you rather than the next result. These pages load in a blink, put a call bar under the thumb on a phone and answer the question the customer typed into Google. The only animation is the one that proves a point. Not sure which lane you are? Book a short call. You will hear which kind of site your customers actually respond to, and whether you need one at all. ### What I build for service businesses — https://thomasrgriffiths08-blip.github.io/skales/what-i-do/

Websites, booking follow-up for trades | Skales Skip to content s k ales --:--:-- UK sheet 36 builds Websites 12 Tools 24 What I do Why Notes Workings Book a call Websites 12 Tools 24 What I do Why Notes Book a call Free teardown Show the workings Off · On What I do Three systems All running below Websites, booking and follow-up for service businesses. Skales builds three things for UK service businesses plumbers, electricians, roofers, fitters, cleaners, salons, anyone whose work comes in by phone: a website that captures the enquiry, booking and a pipeline that chase themselves, and follow-up that runs without you. Every one is running on this page. 01 Capture Websites that capture the enquiry What is a website that captures the enquiry? A capture website is a fast, hand-built site whose only job is to turn a visit into a name and a number. A hand-built website for a service business: three fields, one-tap call, loads before they blink, and every page written to answer the question the customer typed into Google. Built so a visit becomes a name and a number you can ring back. Turnover before and after a rebuild Its page Powering up Drag the tape line across the same roofing firm its 2011 site on one side, the rebuild on the other. Three fields and a one-tap call. Online booking lets the customer take a slot themselves, from a grid generated off your real calendar, and pay a deposit that holds it. Online booking with slots generated from a real calendar, deposits that hold them, quotes that chase themselves, and a pipeline where every enquiry sits with what happened to it. Quotes get chased on a schedule, by the system, not by you at 10pm. 03 Follow up Follow-up that runs itself What does missed-call text-back and review automation do? Missed-call text-back sends a message to a caller you could not answer, seconds after the ring-out, and turns the voicemail into a conversation. A missed call gets a text back in under a minute. A finished job gets a review request the same day. Next year the customer gets a you are due a service reminder. Text-back fires automatically, under a minute after the missed call. It asks one question, so the customer replies instead of shopping around. Review requests go out the day the job is done, while they are still pleased. You re due a service reminders next year, without anyone remembering. ### Own it. Don’t rent it. — https://thomasrgriffiths08-blip.github.io/skales/why/

Why — one person, built in public, you own it | Skales Skip to content s k ales --:--:-- UK sheet 36 builds Websites 12 Tools 24 What I do Why Notes Workings Book a call Websites 12 Tools 24 What I do Why Notes Book a call Free teardown Show the workings Off · On Why One person Built in public Own it. Don t rent it. Skales exists because most service businesses are renting their own website from whoever built it, and getting a brochure for the money. This page is the reasoning, and the straight answers. Ownership Yours from day one Why should you own your own website? You should own your website because it is where your work comes from, and anything that important should not depend on a monthly payment to the person who built it. With Skales, the domain, the code and every account sit in the client s name from the first day. Some builders charge every month, forever, just to keep a site alive. A page-builder account the site cannot leave, a domain registered in the agency s name, a platform fee each one is a lever, and it only gets pulled one way. Every build here is hand-coded, hosted in an account the client controls, with the domain registered to the client. Sack Tom Griffiths tomorrow and everything keeps working. * If a quote includes a monthly platform fee to keep your own site online, that is rent. Walk away. One person No account manager Who builds it? Tom Griffiths does. Skales is one person, based in the United Kingdom, and the person you message is the person who does the work. There is no sales call handed to a junior, and nothing gets lost in a handover because there is not one. Operator Tom Griffiths. Builds every site and system personally. Base United Kingdom. Built for how UK service businesses get work: the phone, Google, word of mouth. Cadence One system a week, built in public on Instagram (@tomxsystems) . Method Hand-coded. No page-builders, no themes, no stock imagery, no third-party runtime. Proof Thirty-six working builds on the Work page , every one open to use. Contact thomasrgriffiths08@gmail.com book a call In public Watch the next one Why build in public? Because it is the only honest portfolio. A logo wall proves someone paid; a build made in front of you proves what was built. Skales makes one system a week in public, and the sixteen on this site are the result all for invented businesses, so no client s numbers are ever on show. Updated September 2026. Straight answers The questions people ask Questions people ask Skales Do I actually own the website? Yes. With Skales the domain, the code and the hosting sit in your own accounts from day one. It is set up so you could walk away tomorrow and lose nothing; that is the whole point. Is there a monthly fee to keep my site online? No. Skales does not charge a monthly platform fee to keep your own website alive. You pay for hosting and your domain directly, in your own name, at cost. If any quote you get includes a monthly fee to keep your own site online, that is rent. How long does a build take? A capture website takes days. A full system with booking and follow-up usually takes one to two weeks. You get a date with the quote, and you can watch it being built in public. Are the thirty-six builds on this site real clients? No, and deliberately so. Every business, person, review and phone number in the demonstration builds is invented, so nothing on this site exposes anyone Skales works with. They are real working software, just for businesses that do not exist. Who actually does the work? Tom Griffiths. Skales is one person: there is no account manager and no handover to a junior. The person you message is the person who builds it. What kind of businesses is this for? UK service businesses whose work comes in by phone: plumbers, heating engineers, electricians, roofers, kitchen fitters, landscapers, cleaners, salons and similar trades and local operators. What happens after I book a call or send the form? Tom Griffiths looks at your website, your Google listing and what happens when someone tries to reach you, then messages you three things: what is leaking, what to fix first, and what it is worth in jobs. If you want it fixed, you get a flat quote. If not, you keep the list. Do you use page-builders or templates? No. Every build is hand-coded with no page-builder, no theme and no third-party runtime dependencies. Every visual is drawn in code rather than bought from a stock library. Ready when you are. A short call, no pitch. If Skales is the wrong fit you will hear that on the call too. ### What a missed call actually costs a service business — https://thomasrgriffiths08-blip.github.io/skales/notes/what-a-missed-call-costs/

What a missed call actually costs a service business Skip to content s k ales --:--:-- UK sheet 36 builds Websites 12 Tools 24 What I do Why Notes Workings Book a call Websites 12 Tools 24 What I do Why Notes Book a call Free teardown Show the workings Off · On Home / Notes 3 September 2026 Tom Griffiths What a missed call actually costs a service business The sum behind the missed-call text-back, with every assumption on the table — and why the number survives a sceptic. A missed call costs a service business more than the job on the other end of it, because the customer who rang is usually ringing the next firm on the list within the hour. The Stopcock calculator on this site meters that leak from five numbers you already know: calls per week, the share you miss, the value of an average job, how many quotes turn into work, and the share of missed callers who are gone for good. Why the model has a "gone for good" factor Most missed-call calculators quietly assume every missed caller would have booked. They would not. Some ring back, some were price-checking, some booked elsewhere before you saw the voicemail. Stopcock makes that share an explicit slider, so the headline figure is a floor a sceptical owner can defend, not a marketing number. What a text-back in under a minute changes A missed-call text-back sends the customer a message seconds after the ring-out, asks one question, and turns a voicemail into a conversation. The customer who was about to dial the next number replies instead. The follow-up automation on this site does exactly that, and the Redgate demo on the Why page shows the sequence end to end. Open the calculator, put your own numbers in, and argue with it. That is what it is for. Here is what you own it actually means in practice. A website built by this studio belongs to the business it was built for: the domain, the code and every account sit in the client’s name from the first day. A screenshot of a client site cannot do that, and a client site should not be handed to strangers to click through. What a real build shares with these The approach is identical: hand-coded, no page-builder, no stock imagery, built to do one job for one kind of business, and owned outright by the client. The only difference is whose name is on it.
